clue.text: Perhaps a lead sought for Forster heroine

indicators.note: Perhaps suggests the letters of 'a lead' could be arranged some other way

parts.note: sought means looked for, quested

explanation.surface: Someone hunts for a leading lady to play a Forster character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' rearranges A LEAD into ADELA. Adela Quested is the young Englishwoman in E. M. Forster's A Passage to India.
explanation.definitionFit: She is the central female character of Forster's novel A Passage to India.

clue.text: A note on poetry may be unfavourable

parts.note: D is a note of the musical scale
poetry is verse

explanation.surface: A remark added to a poem might be a hostile one.
explanation.definitionFit: Adverse conditions or criticism are hostile and unfavourable.

clue.text: General adaptation to explain more fully

indicators.note: an adaptation of a word reshapes it, so the letters of General are reordered

explanation.surface: A broad rewrite is offered to give a fuller account.
explanation.walkthrough: 'adaptation' rearranges GENERAL; to enlarge on something is to say more about it.
explanation.definitionFit: To enlarge upon a topic is to expand or elaborate on it.

clue.text: Demon seen in remains of fire, thanks to the great American novel writer

parts.note: ash is what is left after a fire
TA is informal British for thank you
Philip Roth wrote a novel called The Great American Novel

explanation.surface: A devil is glimpsed in the embers, courtesy of a celebrated American author.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase looks like praise for any US novelist, but it points to Philip Roth, whose 1973 book is titled The Great American Novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Ashtaroth is a fallen spirit named among Milton's devils and in demonology.

clue.text: This servitude makes you to keep (The Comedy of Errors)

definitions.text: This servitude makes you to keep (The Comedy of Errors)

parts.words: This servitude makes you to keep (The Comedy of Errors)
parts.note: the clue quotes Luciana's line in Shakespeare's play with its last word missing; the solver supplies the word that ends it

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's Comedy of Errors waiting to be completed.
explanation.walkthrough: In Act 2 Scene 1 Luciana tells Adriana that this servitude keeps her from marrying; the gap is the word for not married.
explanation.definitionFit: The line ends by saying the servitude keeps her single, without a husband.

clue.text: Master builder might give lessons

indicators.note: might give says the letters of lessons could yield another word once reordered

explanation.surface: A skilled builder could offer some tuition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might give' rearranges LESSONS. Halvard Solness is the title character of Ibsen's play The Master Builder.
explanation.definitionFit: Solness is Ibsen's architect, the master builder of the play's title.

clue.text: Some revel in a work influencing Jane Austen

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Some readers delight in a book that shaped Jane Austen.
explanation.definitionFit: Fanny Burney's 1778 novel Evelina was an acknowledged influence on Austen's fiction.

clue.text: May Sinclair's Chekhovian siblings (57)

explanation.surface: Two literary sets of sisters, one English and one Russian.
explanation.walkthrough: May Sinclair's 1914 novel and Chekhov's play share this title; the printed (57) is the enumeration (5,7) misread.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinclair's novel and Chekhov's play are both titled after a trio of female siblings.

clue.text: Hot Spanish medieval walled city hot! Suggesting ancient land of gold in Arabia

definitions.text: ancient land of gold in Arabia

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hot on taps
Avila in Castile is famous for its complete medieval walls
H again stands for hot

explanation.surface: A sweltering walled Spanish city evokes a gold-rich biblical land.
explanation.walkthrough: Havilah is the land in Genesis 2 where there is gold; AVILA is a walled city west of Madrid.
explanation.definitionFit: Genesis describes Havilah as a region where gold is found, usually placed in Arabia.

clue.text: Goethe's boss

parts.note: Goethe's novel hero is called Meister, German for master or boss; the clue asks for the first name that goes with him

explanation.surface: Who was Goethe's employer?
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests Goethe's patron, but it points to his novel Wilhelm Meister, whose surname means master.
explanation.definitionFit: The hero of Goethe's novels about apprenticeship and travels is named Wilhelm Meister.

clue.text: Nobel laureate shows GI mule lost on thoroughfare in Port of Spain

indicators.note: lost suggests the words GI mule have gone astray and come out jumbled

parts.note: a street is a thoroughfare, and this one is in the Trinidad capital

explanation.surface: A Nobel winner displays an American soldier's mule gone missing on a Trinidad road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lost' rearranges GIMULE into MIGUEL. Miguel Street is V. S. Naipaul's book of linked stories set in Port of Spain, Trinidad.
explanation.definitionFit: Naipaul, winner of the 2001 Nobel Prize in Literature, wrote this book, so the definition names it by its author.

clue.text: Wedgwood factory in ancient Italy

explanation.surface: A pottery works in old Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: Josiah Wedgwood named his Staffordshire works after the Etruscan region, a part of ancient central Italy.

clue.text: Warwick author

parts.note: this reads like a writer from the English town, but Warwick is a first name; the clue wants the surname of the novelist so called

explanation.surface: A writer from Warwick.
explanation.walkthrough: Warwick Deeping wrote the bestseller Sorrell and Son (1925); Warwick is also a town in central England.
explanation.definitionFit: The popular interwar novelist bore the first name Warwick.

clue.text: A good investment by O'Brien

annotationWithheld.why: A good investment by O'Brien (5): 'investment' fits a siege, but no O'Brien work with this title could be confirmed, so the second half cannot be explained

clue.text: Exaggerate deliveries at gallery

parts.note: in cricket an over is a set of six deliveries by a bowler
the Tate is a London art gallery

explanation.surface: Someone makes too much of the bowling at an art museum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deliveries' sounds like post but is cricket bowling; an over is six balls.
explanation.definitionFit: To overstate is to claim more than the truth, to inflate a point.

clue.text: Lift for ballerina in front of building

explanation.surface: A dancer's jump in front of a theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: In ballet it means the height of a leap; in architecture it is a drawing of one face of a building.

clue.text: Grave work of Herbert

explanation.surface: A serious poem by a metaphysical poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grave' looks like an adjective, but it is the noun for a tomb; George Herbert's poem Sepulchre is in The Temple.
explanation.definitionFit: A tomb cut in rock is a burial place, and Herbert's poem in The Temple carries that title.

clue.text: Apostle in a name for Hadrian's mother and sister

definitions.text: name for Hadrian's mother and sister

parts.note: St Paul is called the Apostle to the Gentiles
taken as written

explanation.surface: An apostle in a name shared by an emperor's mother and sister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a container signal, but it is simply spelt out. Hadrian's mother was Domitia Paulina, and his sister Aelia Domitia Paulina.
explanation.definitionFit: Both women in the emperor's family bore this Roman female name.

clue.text: Short literature may be real, and strictly interpreted

parts.note: lit is a common clipped form of literature

indicators.note: may be suggests the word real is in another possible form, its letters reordered

explanation.surface: Brief writing may be true and read word for word.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be' rearranges REAL into ERAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A literal reading takes the words in their exact sense, with no figurative stretch.

clue.text: German informer who exposed rats?

explanation.surface: A German who betrayed traitors.
explanation.walkthrough: GRASS is British slang for a police informer, who exposes 'rats'; Günter Grass, German novelist, wrote The Rat (Die Rättin).
explanation.definitionFit: Günter Grass was a German writer, and in British slang an informer is a grass.

clue.text: He wrote short stories in his golden age

definitions.text: He wrote short stories in his golden age

parts.words: He wrote short stories in his golden age
parts.note: seems to describe a writer at his peak, but The Golden Age is the title of a book of childhood stories by the Wind in the Willows author

explanation.surface: A writer produced stories at the height of his powers.
explanation.walkthrough: Kenneth Grahame's The Golden Age (1895) is a collection of stories about childhood.
explanation.definitionFit: Kenneth Grahame published the story collection The Golden Age before his famous riverbank novel.

clue.text: Happily dropped by Miss Doolittle

parts.note: Eliza in Pygmalion says 'appily, losing the first letter; the clue asks for the name of that dropped letter, in the plural

explanation.surface: Eliza Doolittle cheerfully abandons something.
explanation.walkthrough: Eliza Doolittle of Shaw's Pygmalion speaks Cockney, which drops the H sound at the start of words.
explanation.definitionFit: The spoken names of the letter H are what a Cockney omits.

clue.text: "Mountains big with mines, / That on the high ridgy rise" (James Thomson)

definitions.text: "Mountains big with mines, / That on the high ridgy rise" (James Thomson)

parts.words: "Mountains big with mines, / That on the high ridgy rise" (James Thomson)
parts.note: the lines from Thomson's poem The Seasons have a word missing after 'high'; the solver supplies it

explanation.surface: A quotation from James Thomson about mountains rich in ore, with a gap.
explanation.walkthrough: In Summer, Thomson pictures tropical mountains rising on the line round the middle of the earth.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomson's full line places the mountains on the great circle midway between the poles.

clue.text: I have something else / To for your good" (Jonson, Volpone)

definitions.text: I have something else / To for your good" (Jonson, Volpone)

parts.words: I have something else / To for your good" (Jonson, Volpone)
parts.note: the lines from Jonson's comedy have one word missing after 'To'; the solver supplies it

explanation.surface: A quotation from Volpone with a gap.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening quotation mark is missing from the clue as printed; the word to supply means bring to maturity.
explanation.definitionFit: The speaker has something else to bring to full readiness for the hearer's benefit.

clue.text: Publicity more suitable for one modifying novel for tv?

parts.note: an ad is publicity for a product
apter is the comparative of apt, more suitable

explanation.surface: Is better publicity needed by a screenwriter dramatising a book?
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who turns a book into a screenplay is said to adapt it for television.

clue.text: The narrator sprang to Roland's, shortened it, later stood in it

definitions.text: The narrator sprang to Roland's, shortened it, later stood in it

parts.words: The narrator sprang to Roland's, shortened it, later stood in it
parts.note: recalls three moments in Browning's poem of the ride from Ghent to Aix, where the rider mounts, adjusts his saddle gear and rises in it

explanation.surface: Episodes from a famous galloping ride.
explanation.walkthrough: In Browning's How They Brought the Good News from Ghent to Aix, the narrator 'sprang to the stirrup', 'shortened each stirrup', and later 'stood up in the stirrup'; Roland is his horse.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the footrest hanging from a saddle, which a rider mounts by and stands in.

clue.text: His name features in Scott's lists

definitions.text: His name features in Scott's lists

parts.words: His name features in Scott's lists
parts.note: 'lists' looks like inventories, but it means the enclosed ground for a tournament, where Scott's disinherited knight jousts

explanation.surface: A man's name appears on Scott's rolls.
explanation.walkthrough: The lists are the jousting ground; the hero of Scott's novel triumphs at the Ashby tournament and gives the book its title.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilfred of the title is the knight who fights in the tournament in Scott's 1819 romance.
